bugs: Bug of the Day: Python is not named after the snake - Guido van Rossum named it after Monty Python's Flying Circus, the comedy group. So never blame the reptile for your syntax error.
Bug of the Day: Naming your own file time.py (or any module name) can shadow Python's real module, so 'import time' starts loading YOUR file instead. Your code then fails in a very confusing way.
Bug of the Day: A classic off-by-one error happens because counting starts at 0, so range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 - beginners happily wait for the number 5 that never arrives.

Bug of the Day: == compares two values while = assigns one, so writing if x == 5 = 3 by habit can silently change your variable instead of checking it. Two tiny symbols, two completely different jobs.

Bug of the Day: In 1996 a rocket veered off course because a big number was squeezed into a smaller space and lost precision. Overflow errors were breaking things long before your Python homework did.
Bug of the Day: The Y2K worry was really an off-by-two-digits problem: years were stored as 99, and some systems turned the year 2000 back into 1900.
Bug of the Day: A missing colon, or a stray tab where spaces belong, can stop Python in its tracks. Whitespace is part of the language here, not decoration.
Bug of the Day: Heisenbugs are bugs that vanish the moment you look at them - printing a variable to debug it can change the timing that caused the problem in the first place.
Bug of the Day: One famous trading software glitch was caused by old, disabled code that was switched back on years later. Dead code can wake up and misbehave.
Bug of the Day: += and + are not twins for lists: x += [1] edits the original list, while x = x + [1] builds a brand-new one and leaves any alias pointing at the old data.
Bug of the Day: In real floating point math 0.1 + 0.2 prints as 0.30000000000000004, because computers store decimals in binary and simply cannot represent some numbers exactly.
Bug of the Day: Forgetting the brackets - writing print(len) instead of print(len(x)) - happily prints something like <built-in function len> and baffles everyone reading your output.
Bug of the Day: A default argument like def greet(name, tags=[]) remembers whatever you append to that list between calls, so the list quietly grows for every new call.
Bug of the Day: Copy-pasting a block of code and forgetting to change one variable is the classic beginner bug - the program runs perfectly and always uses the old value.
Bug of the Day: The very first software bug was famously a moth stuck inside a machine in 1947. The team literally taped the insect into their logbook as the first entry.
Bug of the Day: Typos inside a string, like 'maths' vs 'math', never raise any error at all - you just end up with a key that nothing else in the program will ever find.
didYouKnow: Did you know? Typing import this prints the Zen of Python, a short poem of guiding principles like 'Simple is better than complex'. It was hidden in Python as an Easter egg by Tim Peters.
Did you know? Python is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, the comedy group, and not after the snake at all.
Did you know? Underscores can separate digits for readability, so 1_000_000 is just one million - very handy when you print big counts.
Did you know? Dictionaries have kept the order of their keys since Python 3.7, so insertion order is now guaranteed rather than a lucky side effect.
Did you know? Tuples are a little faster and use less memory than lists, and because they cannot change they can be used as dictionary keys, while lists cannot.
Did you know? None is a singleton - there is only ever one None object in your whole program, which is why Python suggests comparing with is None.
Did you know? Strings are immutable, so a method like s.upper() builds a brand-new string instead of changing the old one. That is why you must save the result back.
Did you know? enumerate() hands you a counter as you loop, so for i, name in enumerate(names): starts counting at 0 with no extra bookkeeping.
Did you know? zip() stitches lists together, pairing the first items, then the second, and so on - perfect for looping over two lists at the same time.
Did you know? pass is a do-nothing statement that exists so you can write an empty block, like a function you have not finished yet, without a syntax error.
Did you know? Python uses indentation to define blocks, so the language itself forces your code to look neat - there are no curly braces you can forget.
Did you know? Duck typing means 'if it behaves like a duck, it is a duck' - Python cares more about what an object can do than about what type it claims to be.
Did you know? PEP 8 is Python's style guide, recommending things like snake_case for function names so everyone's code looks familiar to everyone else.
Did you know? Python 2 reached its end of life in 2020 and Python 3 has been the standard for years - some older tutorials still show print 'hi' without brackets.
Did you know? f-strings like f'{name} is {age}' arrived in Python 3.6 after years of debate about formatting, and they are now the favourite way to build text.
Did you know? The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) means one Python process runs one thread at a time, which is why Python reaches for processes for heavy parallel work.
Did you know? The walrus operator := gets its name from the tusks it resembles, and it lets you assign and use a value in the same line. It arrived in Python 3.8.
Did you know? list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, so writing x = mylist.sort() empties x into None - a favourite beginner trap.
Did you know? Guido van Rossum started Python in the early 1990s as a holiday project, proving that even language legends code during their breaks.
Did you know? Python compiles your code to bytecode first and caches it in __pycache__ folders, which is why the second run of a script often starts faster.
